title: Similarly built animals should jump to the same absolute height regardless of size

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Similarly built animals should jump to the same absolute height regardless of size

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Because the impulse of a leap is proportional to muscle volume and so to body mass, the take-off velocity is independent of size, and similarly built animals should jump to the same actual height rather than the same relative height; longer levers in larger animals give them some advantage.

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: impulse \propto M \Rightarrow v_0 independent of L; jump height h = v_0^2/2g independent of L

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: in other words, that all animals, provided always that they are similarly fashioned, with their various levers etc., in like proportion, ought to jump, not to the same relative, but to the same actual height.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter II, “On Magnitude”; topic “Leaping and size”. Scope: jumping animals of similar construction across sizes, from fleas to horses

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: impulse \propto M \Rightarrow v_0 independent of L; jump height h = v_0^2/2g independent of L

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch02-09: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.65

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The predicted exponent and outcome are unambiguous, and published public trait records permit a restricted comparative test. Coverage from fleas to horses with matched geometry is inadequate, requiring substantial compilation for the full scope.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compile maximal jump height, body length and limb geometry for similarly constructed animals, then test whether absolute height has a size exponent of zero after controlling lever ratios. A consistent nonzero scaling exponent would refute the stated law.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Finding animals that satisfy similar construction across a wide size range is difficult.

Jump-height measurements are sparse and methodologically heterogeneous.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
operationalizability: 0.9
data existence: 0.55
discriminating power: 0.7
data adequacy: 0.45
analysis feasibility: 0.65

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Absolute versus relative jump height is a sharp, measurable contrast, so operationalizability and discriminating power are high. The obstacle is the data: published jump performances would have to be compiled, they do not span the flea-to-horse range under a common protocol, and similar construction is a judgment rather than a column in a table. Existing numbers can test a mammal subset after months of harmonization, which is only a partial resolution.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Regress absolute jump height, or take-off velocity, on body length for animals judged similarly proportioned. A slope near zero for absolute height, together with a negative slope for height relative to body length, would support the claim; height proportional to size would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Jump height against size, from small jumpers to large mammals, is scattered through papers rather than held in one public dataset.

Elastic tendons and crouched postures violate the similar-construction premise and change the expected scaling.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
operationalizability: 0.8
discriminating power: 0.65
analysis feasibility: 0.4
data adequacy: 0.35
data existence: 0.4
